issue.issue_text: Whether the respondent was obligated under the Code of Civil Procedure to plead in his written statement that a meeting occurred on February 6, 1967, when the appellant's petition only alleged a meeting on February 7, 1967.

facts: The appellant's petition alleged that a meeting was held on February 7, 1967.
In his written statement, the respondent denied that a meeting was held on that date.

The appellant argued that the respondent was obligated under the Code of Civil Procedure to affirmatively state that a meeting had actually occurred on February 6, 1967, and that the failure to do so denied the appellant the opportunity to counter that claim.
law: The appellant cited the precedent of *Hadar & Company v. F. I. Trading*, where the Supreme Court held that a mere denial of a contract was insufficient and that the defendant was required to specifically deny the existence of letters alleged by the plaintiff.
The relevant procedural rules are contained in Order VIII of the Code of Civil Procedure, which governs written statements.
application: The Supreme Court distinguished the current case from the *Hadar & Company* precedent.
The Court noted that in *Hadar & Company*, the defendant failed to specifically deny evidence (letters) that the plaintiff had alleged in their claim.
In the present case, the specific question raised by the appellant's petition was whether a meeting occurred on February 7, 1967.
The respondent directly answered this question by denying it.
The Court reasoned that the respondent was only called upon to answer the specific allegation made against him, which concerned a meeting on February 7.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court rejected the appellant's argument, concluding that the respondent was not obligated to plead that a meeting occurred on February 6, 1967. The respondent's only duty was to respond to the specific allegation in the petition, which he did by denying that a meeting took place on February 7, 1967.

issue.issue_text: Whether the publication of a document (Annexure KK) was done with the consent of the respondent or his election agent, thereby constituting a corrupt practice under section 123(3A) or 123(4) of the Representation of the People Act, 1951.

facts: The appellant alleged that the respondent, Prakash Vir Shastri, committed a corrupt practice by publishing a document referred to as Annexure KK.
The appellant contended that the upper portion of Annexure KK amounted to communal propaganda and the lower portion contained false allegations against the appellant's personal character.
law: For a publication to be a corrupt practice under section 123(4) of the Representation of the People Act, 1951, it must be published with the consent of the candidate or their election agent.
A corrupt practice under section 123(3A) involves promoting feelings of enmity or hatred on grounds of religion.
application: The Court found that the appellant failed to prove that Annexure KK was published with the consent of the respondent or his election agent.
The Court also noted that "Anncxure KK was not proved," meaning the appellant failed to properly evidence the document itself.

As a result of these failures of proof, the Court determined that the document could not be said to constitute communal propaganda or an attack on the appellant's personal character attributable to the respondent.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court rejected the appellant's claim, concluding that because it was not established that Annexure KK was published with the consent of the respondent or his agent, its publication did not constitute a corrupt practice under either section 123(3A) or 123(4) of the Act.

issue.issue_text: Whether a meeting was held at the Town Hall Maidan at Hapur on February 7, 1967, as alleged by the appellant.

facts: The appellant alleged that a meeting was held in support of the respondent at the Town Hall Maidan in Hapur on February 7, 1967.
The respondent denied that such a meeting took place on that date.
Both sides presented conflicting oral testimony from witnesses.
The appellant relied on newspaper reports from the 'Hindustan' and 'Vir Arjun' as evidence.

Other documentary evidence included an application for a meeting permit, a police diary, and a First Information Report filed by the appellant's supporters regarding a separate incident on the same day.
law: In cases of conflicting oral testimony, it is safer to place reliance on documentary evidence.
application: The Court analyzed the appellant's own documentary evidence and found it unconvincing. The 'Hindustan' newspaper report, dated Feb 8, referred to a meeting held "yesterday night," which would mean February 6, not February 7.
Another newspaper, 'Vir Arjun', mentioned a meeting but did not specify the date it was held.

Conversely, other documents strongly suggested that the meeting held on February 7 was for the rival Congress Party. These included an application for a permit (Exhibit A-12), the permission granted (Exhibit A-B), and a police diary entry (Exhibit A-2) mentioning a Congress speaker.
The Court found it "highly improbable" that two meetings of rival candidates would be held on the same date and at the same place.

Crucially, reports filed by the appellant's own supporters about an alleged attack on their party office on February 7 were "significantly silent" about any meeting being held by the respondent on that day. The Court found this omission unnatural if such a meeting had actually occurred.
The testimony of the respondent's witnesses, who stated that a Congress meeting took place on that day, was consistent with the documentary evidence.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court rejected the appellant's claim, concluding that the documentary evidence contradicted the allegation. The evidence indicated that the meeting held on February 7, 1967, was organized by the rival Congress Party, not by the respondent's supporters.

cases.case_name: Guruji Shrihar Baliram Jivatode v. Vithalrao and Others
cases.principle: To explain the scope and content of sub-section (4) of section 123 of the Representation of the People Act, which is intended to protect freedom of speech on one hand and restrain malicious propaganda on the other.

That in reading election documents, it is unrealistic to ignore that appeals by candidates contain partisan feeling and extravagance of expression, and the court must consider the effect of a pamphlet on the mind of the ordinary voter.

ratio_decidendi.ratio: Under the Code of Civil Procedure, a defendant's denial of a plaintiff's specific factual allegation is sufficient; the defendant is not required to plead an alternative version of the facts in their written statement to be permitted to introduce evidence that contradicts the plaintiff's allegation.
obiter: In the case of conflicting oral testimony, it is safer to place reliance on documentary evidence.

judicial_reasoning.core_finding: The court concluded that the appellant failed to meet the burden of proof for the alleged corrupt practices. Specifically, the appellant did not establish that the respondent consented to the publication of a key document (Annexure KK), and the appellant's own documentary evidence contradicted the claim that a specific meeting took place, making the oral testimony unreliable.
legal_tests_applied: For a statement to be a corrupt practice under section 123(4), it must be a false statement of fact that "pierces the politician and touches the person of the candidate," bearing on their personal character and conduct, and it must be reasonably calculated to prejudice their election prospects.

Under section 123(3A), a corrupt practice involves the promotion of, or attempt to promote, feelings of enmity or hatred between different classes of citizens on grounds of religion, race, caste, community, or language.
In the case of conflicting oral testimony, it is safer to place reliance on documentary evidence.
When evaluating election materials, courts must consider "what the effect of the pamphlet would be on the mind of the ordinary voter who reads the pamphlet."
why_appellant_lost: The appellant failed to prove that the publication of Annexure KK was done with the consent of the respondent or his election agent, which is a necessary element to establish a corrupt practice under section 123.
Regarding the alleged meeting at Hapur on February 7, 1967, the newspaper report on which the appellant relied contained intrinsic evidence that "totally nullifies the appellant's case."

The court found the appellant's oral evidence regarding various allegations unacceptable, noting that the absence of any report to the Election Commission or police authorities was an "important and noticeable feature."
why_respondent_won: The appellant failed to establish that Annexure KK was published with the consent of the respondent or his election agent.

The respondent's position that the meeting on February 7, 1967, was not held was effectively proven by the contradictions within the appellant's own documentary evidence, which the court preferred over conflicting oral testimony.
policy_considerations: In reading election documents, "it would be unrealistic to ignore that when appeals are made by candidate there is an element of 'partisan feeling', and there is 'extravagance of expression in attacking one another'."
